JSON in plain English

An API is a door with rules. You knock with a request. You get a response, usually a bundle of labelled boxes called JSON. “Give me this shop.” “Make this customer.” “Here is the weather.” You do not have to love the word. You have to know which door you are knocking on and what you sent.

A webhook is the opposite direction. They knock on you. Stripe says paid. GitHub says pushed. Shopify says the order changed. Your URL has to be awake and honest about what it received.

How to think about it

Write the sentence first. “When a shop goes quiet, draft the usual order.” That sentence hides two doors: one you call (Shopify), one that calls you (a schedule, or a webhook). Grok can write the knock. You still have to read the reply when it is rude.

How I actually do it

This site’s save endpoint is a tiny API. The browser posts. The function writes to GitHub. Send Reorder is almost all other people’s APIs glued together with taste. Meeting Mode will knock on a calendar. None of that is magic. It is doors and keys and logs.

Where noobs get stuck

Calling something an API because it is fashionable. Or never logging the payload, then wondering why nothing happens. Or exposing an endpoint that does dangerous work with no secret at all.

Film this

One request in, one JSON out, read aloud like a shopping list. Then a webhook: a test ping, a log line, a row that appeared because someone else knocked.

Do this before chapter 15

  • Call one public API and print one field you care about.
  • Write one endpoint that accepts a POST and logs the body.
  • Put a secret on anything that can write.
